full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** I'd call it high-to-medium confidence. The specific fine-scale details are not checked.

**1. Model family.** This is active matter, specifically self-propelled particles with non-reciprocal, vision-cone, position-based (bearing-based) steering and no velocity alignment. Each particle is a constant-speed agent that turns toward the positions of visible neighbours, with rotational noise. Sometimes this is called a "minimal cognitive flocking model" or an "intelligent active Brownian particle" model.

**2. The behaviour.** Particles that only steer toward what they see (no heading copying) form dense aggregates. They show strong density heterogeneity (CV about 2.1) and nearest-neighbour clumping (ratio 0.44). Global polar order stays low (about 0.07) because there is no alignment rule. This matches the setting of Barberis & Peruani:
- The model has particles with no memory. They interact through a short-ranged, position-based attraction inside a vision cone, and they lack velocity-velocity alignment. The attraction acts inside a vision cone (VC) and the model lacks velocity-velocity alignment.
- Because the VC breaks Newton's third law, the system shows various complex, large-scale, self-organized patterns.
- The title names the pattern types: incidental leaders, nematic patterns and aggregates.

Our "aggregates with weak polarity" outcome falls in that family. The one-sided seeing in the rule system ("being seen does not imply seeing back") is exactly the non-reciprocity that paper emphasises.

**Earliest clear source.** L. Barberis & F. Peruani, "Large-scale patterns in a minimal cognitive flocking model: incidental leaders, nematic patterns, and aggregates," Phys. Rev. Lett. 117, 248001 (2016). I confirmed the title, authors, year and journal via Google Scholar and the reference lists in citing papers. The arXiv version is 1912.07929.

**Later work on closely related systems** (all confirmed in search results):
- "Collective behavior of self-steering active particles with velocity alignment and visual perception," Phys. Rev. Research 6, 013118 (2024). It adds polar alignment to vision-based steering. It reports that when the vision angle is low, very few particles are detected within the VC, no clusters can form, and particles are distributed homogeneously. That is a useful check on the narrow cone (half-angle π/8) here.
- "Collective behavior based on topological vision," Phys. Rev. Research 7, 023234 (2025). It uses a topological neighbourhood instead of a metric one. Its vision breaks the action-reaction symmetry.
- Barberis & Peruani is also cited as the basis for the Springer EPJE 2025 paper "Emergent collective behavior of cohesive, aligning particles" (Eur. Phys. J. E).

I did not find a dedicated review article. The 2024 and 2025 papers serve as the most recent consolidating references.

**Caveats on equivalence.**
- I did not check the exact functional form of the turning rule. Ours is a rate times the mean sine of the bearing angle, which is a standard torque toward the neighbour direction. I did not verify that Barberis & Peruani use the same form.
- Their paper has its own noise convention, speed, density and interaction range. Ours are R = 5, density 1 and speed 0.1, with point particles and no collisions.
- Their phase diagram may place our parameters in the aggregate regime or somewhere else, for example nematic arrays. My confidence that the qualitative behaviour (clumping with no polar order) is known is higher than my confidence about the exact regime.
- I did not read the full text of the 2016 paper, only its abstract and the descriptions in citing papers.
- Two statistics (a_step = 1.855 and a_ang_mom = 0.028) are uninterpreted in the prompt, so I did not try to match them to literature.
